text: Looking steadily at a small spot does not hold the eye perfectly still. [Between brief, rapid movements called [**microsaccades**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"}, the eye makes a small, smooth, irregular movement called fixational drift.]{.definition-explanation} Here drift names the slow eye movement, which can be largely random. Systematic drift in the memory equations instead means a nonzero mean velocity. [Does this movement begin as noise in the muscles, or does the brain send a changing command to them?]{.key-statement} Ben-Shushan and colleagues answer this in two stages. Their recordings support a large shared drive upstream of the motor neurons. Their model then proposes a particular source: random motion of the eye position stored in a memory circuit.[^p2-question]

This distinction connects the previous chapters to a measurement outside the brain. A memory coordinate can diffuse inside a neural network, but the movement produced by that coordinate also depends on the muscles and the mechanics of the eye. We need to follow the signal through those stages before comparing a neural diffusion law with an eye trajectory.

A recording from one motor neuron becomes useful for this comparison only after its spikes and the eye's movement can be expressed on the same scale. The larger movements provide that calibration. Applying it during fixation then lets us ask whether independent motor noise could explain the observed relationship, and estimate the shared contribution under explicit gain and independence assumptions.

The [eye anatomy and motor action](ch-foundations.html#sec-foundations-eye-action) explain why a position must be maintained by an ongoing command. The oculomotor integrator supplies the lasting position signal. In the proposed mechanism, the continuous attractor described in the [foundations](ch-persistence.html#sec-foundations-attractor) and [network model](ch-foundations.html#sec-memory-spikes) stores horizontal eye position. Noise moves the stored value along that attractor.[^p2-pathway]

The signal reaches ocular motoneurons (OMNs), whose spikes activate the eye muscles. [The recordings came from the [**abducens nucleus**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"}, a group of brainstem neurons that includes OMNs activating the lateral rectus muscle, which turns the eye outward.]{.definition-explanation} Other neurons in that nucleus carry signals to other neurons rather than directly to muscle. The study separated these cell types by how their firing changed with eye position and movement. [Finally, the muscles and the mechanical properties of the eye, together called the [**ocular plant**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"}, turn neural activity into movement.]{.definition-explanation}[^p2-recordings]
There are three possible contributions to an observed fixational drift:
- A changing shared command sent to many OMNs. - Private spike variability in individual OMNs. - Variability after those neurons, including muscle and measurement noise.

[Private spike fluctuations can partly cancel when many neurons act together. A common command survives this averaging.]{.key-statement} This is why the noisy activity of one neuron can reveal a source that dominates the much smoother eye movement. The shared drive and common command below mean the signal sent to many OMNs. The variable $C$ later measures its contribution to eye displacement after motor and muscle filtering.

The authors reanalyzed earlier experiments in two male rhesus macaques. With their heads held still, the monkeys first looked at a stationary spot of light on a monitor and then followed the moving spot. A wire search coil on one eye measured the eye's angle while an electrode recorded one neuron's spikes. There were 57 identified OMNs. [Each recording paired one OMN with eye movement. There were no simultaneous recordings of multiple OMNs. Thus the analysis cannot directly measure the covariance between two recorded motor neurons.]{.key-statement}[^p2-recordings][^p2-single]

The initial stationary target was followed by 500–700 ms of required fixation before the target stepped and began moving. Neural voltage was sampled at 25 kHz and eye position at 1 kHz. The authors detected microsaccades using eye speed and acceleration, removed 30 ms on each side of them, and manually checked the remaining segments. For the main displacement analysis, segments shorter than 350 ms were excluded and longer ones were split into nonoverlapping 350 ms pieces. There were 302 such pieces per cell on average, with different counts across cells. These repeated observations improve estimates within two animals. They do not create 57 independent animal samples.[^p2-segments]

The large movements have a useful role even though the scientific question concerns tiny drifts. They produce enough rate change to estimate how each cell's activity depends on eye movement. The fitted relationship is then applied during fixation. This transfer is an assumption to examine, because an incorrect gain during drift would change the inferred common variance. Gain is the scale that converts a change in one signal into a change in the other.

Figure 1c illustrates a weak relationship for one cell. Fig. 1d shows a positive population effect. A silicon circuit can keep a connection strength unchanged while losing the angle it was asked to remember. It can also keep that angle while its individual electrical signals change. To compare electronic memory with the neural memory in Part I, we first need to identify what information each physical quantity represents. This chapter separates the connection settings, the changing state of each artificial neuron, and the value represented by their joint activity. That separation will let us ask what feedback actually preserves.

Imagine giving a circuit a brief cue for an angle of $30^\circ$. After the cue ends, a connected group of artificial neurons remains active. We estimate the remembered angle from which neurons are active and how strongly. The experiment involves:

1. **Connection weights** determine how a signal from one neuron changes another neuron's state. A weight can be fixed throughout the trial. 2. **Neuron and synapse states** change during the trial. Examples include a voltage, a current left by recent inputs, or a number representing either quantity. 3. **The remembered angle** is a property of the joint state, recovered by a readout rule. It need not occupy one dedicated storage cell.

[Keeping the weights unchanged preserves the circuit's rule of operation. Keeping the cue available requires the resulting activity to preserve information about that cue.]{.key-statement} Training can change the first object. Remembering a new angle can change the second and third without any further training.

[[**Neuromorphic computing**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} implements computations inspired by neural circuits using electronic systems organized around neurons, connections, events, or their dynamics.]{.definition-explanation} Some systems calculate neural states as digital numbers. Others use voltages and currents that evolve physically. A system can combine both approaches. The word alone does not tell us where its memory is stored or whether it demonstrates a biological memory mechanism.

[[**Working memory**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"}, in this Part, means keeping information about a recent input available for a later task.]{.definition-explanation} Persistent activity is one candidate mechanism. A slowly decaying state, a sequence of states, or an explicit digital buffer can also store recent information. We must specify the allowed delay and readout error before calling one implementation adequate.
**Example: the same weights can hold different angles.**

Suppose a ring of 32 artificial neurons has fixed local excitation and broader inhibition. A cue near neuron 3 creates a localized group of active neurons there. A later trial cues neuron 11 and creates a group near that location. The same connection weights support both trials. A decoder assigns an angle to the active group's center. If the group moves after the cue, the decoded angle changes even though every stored weight remains correct. This is an example constructed to illustrate the distinction. It is not a specification of a chip.

The neural model still needs a physical implementation. If the model has a variable called membrane voltage, a chip may store it as a binary number or as an actual circuit voltage. Those choices expose the computation to different errors. [[**Current**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} is electric charge flowing per unit time, measured in amperes (coulombs per second).]{.definition-explanation} [[**Voltage**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} is an electrical energy difference per unit charge, measured in volts (joules per coulomb).]{.definition-explanation}

For fixed capacitance $C$, its stored charge $Q$ and voltage difference $V$ satisfy $Q=CV$.]{.definition-explanation} Charge is measured in coulombs and capacitance in farads (coulombs per volt). Supplying current changes $Q$, so it changes the stored voltage.

[[**Digital storage**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} uses distinguishable physical ranges to represent discrete symbols, usually bits.]{.definition-explanation} In [[**static random-access memory (SRAM)**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"}, powered transistor feedback maintains one of two states representing a bit.]{.definition-explanation} Several bits can encode a weight or a changing neuron variable. Reliable bits do not imply unlimited numerical precision: a finite word represents only finitely many values.

[[**Analog state**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} represents a model quantity through the magnitude of a physical variable, such as capacitor voltage.]{.definition-explanation} Input current changes stored charge and so changes voltage. Leakage changes that voltage during a quiet interval. Feedback or new input can oppose the leakage. In BrainScaleS-2, the membrane state evolves this way, while local SRAM stores the synaptic weights.[^hardware-pehle]

[[**Phase-change memory (PCM)**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} stores information in a material's atomic arrangement, including the proportions of ordered and disordered regions, which affect its electrical resistance.]{.definition-explanation} Programming pulses heat the material. Its heating and cooling history changes the arrangement. [[**Conductance**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} measures the current produced per unit applied voltage where current is approximately proportional to voltage. It is the inverse of resistance, the voltage required per unit current.]{.definition-explanation} Reading the conductance can recover a stored weight. Such storage is [[**nonvolatile**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"}: it can retain its state without continuous power, within its retention limits.]{.definition-explanation} Nonvolatile weights can remain after the changing neural state has disappeared.

As $\kappa$ tends to zero, expanding the exponential gives $2Dt$. This is a local model inside one stable state's region of attraction. It does not describe rare switches between digital states or estimate a hardware bit-error rate.

**Interpretation.** Adding restoration to an angle memory can reduce random spread by drawing nearby angles toward preferred positions. That also reduces the set of distinct values retained. [[**Pinning**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} means that imperfections or imposed structure draw a nominally continuous memory toward preferred states.]{.definition-explanation} A flat error variance can mean successful retention near one preferred value while other cues have been biased toward it. Both mean error and spread are needed.

[Burak and Fiete's diffusion bound concerns a specified noisy neural memory model. It is not a lower bound on the error of every electronic memory.]{.key-statement} A digital device that freezes a number, uses explicit error correction, or changes the noise and readout assumptions poses a different problem. To transfer the bound, match the dynamics, noise, available observations, and time scale first.[^dynamics-burak]

A physical demonstration lets us test whether feedback maintains the intended state despite unequal devices and finite resolution. The following early experiments make different claims and should be read separately.

Massoud and Horiuchi built a head-direction circuit whose localized activity could persist after a cue and move with velocity input. It had 32 bump positions around a circle, a spacing of $11.25^\circ$. This demonstrates a physical orientation representation with finite resolution. It does not establish an exact continuum of persistent states or a measured Brownian diffusion law.[^dynamics-massoud]

Giulioni and colleagues built a recurrent spiking circuit with low and high activity states. Brief stimulation could initiate activity lasting seconds despite millisecond circuit dynamics. Their measurements also examined noise-driven transitions and recovery after disturbance. This is [[**bistability**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"}: two locally stable states under the same ongoing conditions.]{.definition-explanation} It supplies a physical working-memory example, but its two-state retention is a different task from retaining an arbitrary angle.[^dynamics-giulioni]

The comparison gives a useful reading rule for current machines: determine what values the network distinguishes, then ask how long and how accurately it preserves them. Neuron count or nonvolatile weight storage cannot answer those questions alone.

Suppose we want to study how a noisy network retains an angle. One machine can calculate every state update as arithmetic. Another can let capacitor voltages perform part of the dynamics. A third can use material conductances to multiply inputs by stored weights. The scientific choice is which physical effects we want to control, measure, or exploit. This chapter compares these implementations and then examines recent demonstrations of memory and learning.

The research snapshot is **October 30, 2026**. “State of the art” here means selected recent capabilities supported by primary papers, with older architecture papers supplying their physical explanation. It does not mean one machine leads every task. We distinguish measured chips, experiments partly run on a separate computer, and proposed hardware evaluated by simulation. A [[**host computer**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} is a separate general-purpose computer that controls an experiment or performs calculations assigned outside the neuromorphic chip.]{.definition-explanation}

A useful platform must make the variables of interest accessible. If the question concerns a specific noise law, a digital update may allow precise control of the injected noise. The following studies make progress on different parts of the memory problem. For each, ask what information persists and which physical component is responsible.

**A useful input history on Loihi 2, 2025.** Kleyko and colleagues implemented a stored history of recent inputs and functions of those inputs that include products. A trained readout uses these values to predict an output. This shows that changing chip state can supply useful information about recent inputs. It is not a measurement of indefinitely stable cue retention. Their pictured Hala Point system is much larger than the resources used in the experiment.[^systems-kleyko]

**Persistent spatial activity on SpiNNaker 2, September 2026.** Aitsam and colleagues ran a 768-neuron recurrent sheet on one chip. A host computer processed the physical event camera's output into a smoothed estimate of the target's center and sent that position to the chip. The configured neural update used deterministic integer-weight dynamics, without an added stochastic neural-noise term. During an eight-second interval without input, the decoded activity center moved by at most half a cell. This establishes persistence for that interval, not a measured lifetime or a test of noise-driven diffusion. During tracking, recurrence reduced frame-to-frame jitter by 15% relative to the host-smoothed input, but added about 115 ms of lag and increased mean position error from 2.02 to 5.65 cells. The robot-guidance evaluation used a simulated robot, and its power figures were estimates. Longer-delay tests with controlled noise would help compare this implementation with the stochastic memory theory.[^systems-aitsam]

**Rapid adaptation using PCM, 2025.** Ortner and colleagues used physical PCM weights for a recurrent spiking network that produced robotic-arm commands after a task-specific update. Earlier training adjusted the model for rapid adaptation to new tasks. The PCM units performed matrix-vector products. Other operations ran on a host computer. This locates the demonstrated advance in weight adaptation and mixed hardware computation. It does not show that PCM cells themselves sustained an autonomous recurrent activity pattern.[^systems-ortner]

**Reduced material drift, online 2025 and in a 2026 issue.** Wang and colleagues measured low resistance drift in a chromium-telluride phase-change material, CrTe$_3$. Reduced drift can help a programmed conductance continue representing the intended weight. Their demonstration of several programmed resistance levels used laser programming and electrical readout. Electrical switching was a separate demonstration. Operation with several levels in nanoscale devices, performance beyond a million programming cycles, and variability across large arrays remained open. This is progress in a storage material, not a complete multilevel neuromorphic processor.[^systems-wang]

[Better temporal state, faster adaptation, and more stable weights solve different problems, so progress in one does not establish the others.]{.key-statement} For the Burak comparison, the missing measurement is often how a decoded value changes during an input-free delay.

Fast spiking units can lose earlier inputs before a later decision needs them. One solution is to add a slower state that summarizes recent activity and sends input back to the fast units. Sun and colleagues' 2026 dual-memory-pathway design takes this route. Their tested slow pathway uses a linear state based on a Legendre memory unit: several stored components summarize the shape of recent input over a sliding time window. It represents a recent input history, rather than a cue held unchanged on a continuous attractor. Its proposed digital hardware holds successive slow states in [[**registers**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"}, small, fast digital storage locations]{.definition-explanation}, and other variables in SRAM. The hardware results came from post-layout simulations, which model a circuit after its physical layout has been designed. They were not measurements of a fabricated chip. The weights were trained before the evaluated tasks.[^systems-sun]

**Example: the update interval determines the physical memory time.**

If updates are separated by $\Delta t$, equating $\alpha^n$ with $e^{-n\Delta t/\tau_m}$ gives $\tau_m=-\Delta t/\ln\alpha$. With $\Delta t=1$ ms and $\alpha=0.999$, $\tau_m$ is about 1 second. After a circuit receives an angle cue, its later estimate may be wrong because the state wandered, because unequal connections pull it toward another angle, or because the observer reads it poorly. One accuracy score combines these causes. The controlled tests below connect these errors to physical parameters. The protocol and reduced models below are proposed tools for reasoning about these experiments, not results already demonstrated on every platform in the previous chapter.

Begin with a circuit whose joint activity represents an angle. Choose a decoder on separate calibration data, then keep it fixed while testing retention. A [[**decoder**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} is a specified rule for estimating the represented quantity from observable circuit signals.]{.definition-explanation} A decoder given every internal state has a different task from a downstream neuron receiving only spikes.
Use the following sequence:

1. Present a brief cue for angle $\theta_0$, then remove it. Test many angles, including values between any suspected preferred positions. 2. Hold the connection weights fixed during each retention trial. Record the actual settings, temperature, update interval, and any imposed noise. 3. Repeat trials at several delays $t$ and decode $\hat\theta(t)$. Use a common reference for angular differences. [[**Unwrapping**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} tracks crossings of $0^\circ/360^\circ$ by adding or subtracting full turns to continue the trajectory.]{.definition-explanation} Use it only when sampling is frequent enough to identify crossings reliably. 4. Report mean error and error variance separately as functions of cue and delay. Also report failures in which the activity pattern disappears or changes form. 5. Repeat with changed noise, calibration, or numerical precision, changing one factor at a time. Compare with the same model running in a numerical reference implementation.

Record the decoded state immediately after each cue so that error in writing the value can be separated from error accumulated during retention. Report the number of repeated trials and uncertainty in the estimated drift and diffusion.

A changed component affects memory through the circuit's equations. Increasing a leak current can shorten a component time constant. Changing a recurrent weight can alter restoration or introduce a preferred angle. A fluctuating current can perturb many neurons, yet only part of the resulting activity change remains as a change of the remembered angle.

**Example: a tighter distribution can hide a biased memory.**

Consider two illustrative circuits after a one-second delay. Circuit A has zero mean angular error and variance $4$ deg$^2$. Circuit B has mean error $3^\circ$ and variance $1$ deg$^2$, because it is attracted toward a preferred angle. Their mean squared errors are $4$ and $1+3^2=10$ deg$^2$. The source papers supply different constraints on this hardware experiment.

- **Burak and Fiete (2012):** compare diffusion with the information available in spikes under matched noise, dynamics, and observation assumptions. A processor that stores an exact internal angle and exposes it directly to the decoder has changed the readout problem. - **Ben-Shushan and colleagues (2022):** a measured output can filter the internal command. Camera exposure, output smoothing, or a mechanical actuator can change the observed motion. Calibrate that path before assigning an output time scale to the memory circuit itself.

- **Mainali and colleagues (2025):** patterns of firing across physical positions constrain a spatial representation. Reproducing field-size statistics does not by itself show that a network implemented in hardware retains position without input. Spatial structure and temporal persistence need separate tests.

These links concern the tested mechanisms, not a claim that a chip reproduces the animal systems. The [synthesis chapter](ch-synthesis.html#sec-synthesis-evidence) sets out the evidence supplied by the original papers.

Time conversion is especially important for accelerated hardware. If model time $t_m=a t_p$, where $t_p$ is physical time and $a>1$ is the acceleration factor, a diffusion law $\operatorname{Var}(\Delta\theta)=2D_m t_m$ becomes $2(aD_m)t_p$. The result is $D_p=aD_m$ when expressed per physical second. This is a change of units for the same ideal trajectory. Physical communication delay, temperature drift, or limited readout speed can prevent a real device from obeying that ideal rescaling.

For an energy comparison, specify the cue distribution, delay, permitted decoding error, and failed-trial rate. Measure energy over writing, waiting, and reading, including required host processing and interfaces. Then report how error and energy change as delay increases. An operations-per-second or operations-per-watt figure alone cannot establish the cost of retaining a useful value.

The resulting research question is concrete: **which part of the physical implementation limits the accuracy of a remembered quantity, and does changing that part improve retention under the same task and readout?** That question turns von Neumann's comparison into a test of contemporary neural and electronic memory mechanisms.
